question.worked_solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

We wish to compute ${J}^{′}(t),$ where

$$
J(t)={\int }_{1}^{3}(5x+t)^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$
{J}^{′}(t)={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(5x+t)^{2}]\,\text{d}x.
$$

Next, let's compute the partial derivative with respect to $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂t}[(5x+t)^{2}] & =2(5x+t)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}(5x+t) \\  & =2(5x+t)\cdot 1 \\  & =2(5x+t)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this back into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}^{′}(t) & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2(5x+t)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{3}(5x+t)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(5x+t)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{3}5x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}t\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{1}^{3}+tx{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =20+2t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}^{′}(t) & =2(20+2t) \\  & =4(t+10).\end{aligned}
$$
